title: Insureksi atau Revolusi?
content:
Saul Newman. Teks aslinya berjudul “Insurrection or Revolution?”. Diterjemahkan ke dalam Bahasa Indonesia oleh Taratsa.

Pada saat narasi besar tentang Revolusi yang kita warisi dari modernitas dan diskursus rasionalis Pencerahan hampir runtuh, apa alternatif yang ada untuk mengonseptualisasikan transformasi radikal? Meski tidak adanya kelas atau gerakan revolusioner yang terorganisir, pada saat yang sama kaum kiri tidak mampu berpikir melampaui gagasan emansipasi revolusioner. Kegagalan imajinasi radikal inilah yang mungkin menjadi alasan kebuntuan politik yang dihadapi kaum kiri saat ini.

Karena tidak mampu menciptakan perubahan yang bermakna, kaum kiri malah terjebak dalam “perang budaya” dan terlibat dalam politik identitas melawan kaum kanan yang jauh lebih terampil memainkan permainan ini. Dogmatisme puritan dan semangat keagamaan yang mengiringi perdebatan tanpa akhir tentang identitas gender, ras, inklusi kaum marginal, dan sebagainya menunjukkan kelelahan tertentu dari horizon politik radikal.

Menjadikan politik didasarkan pada pengakuan identitas, di satu sisi, dan janji masa depan tentang keselamatan revolusioner, di sisi lain, berarti jatuh ke dalam perangkap kekuasaan negara. Negara difetiskan baik sebagai entitas yang memberikan hak dan status hukum kepada minoritas, maupun sebagai musuh yang harus ditaklukkan agar kebebasan dapat diwujudkan—ilusi yang, sebagaimana ditunjukkan oleh sejarah revolusi, hanya menghasilkan negara-negara baru dan bentuk-bentuk despotisme baru.

Mungkin sudah waktunya untuk meninggalkan “bayangan (spooks)” identitas dan revolusi, serta memikirkan subyektivitas dan politik dengan cara yang berbeda. Di sinilah saya mengusulkan untuk kembali pada filsuf anarkis egois abad ke-19, Max Stirner. Dalam karya The Ego and Its Own (Der Einzige und sein Eigentum), yang diterbitkan pada tahun 1844, Stirner mengusulkan bentuk aksi politik alternatif yang ia sebut “Insureksi” (Insurrection atau Empörung), yang ia bandingkan dengan Revolusi.

Jika Revolusi adalah proyek yang bertujuan mengubah hubungan sosial dan politik eksternal, maka insureksi adalah transformasi diri. Ini adalah cara bagi individu untuk mengatasi kepatuhan sukarela dan identifikasinya dengan otoritas. Dengan demikian, insureksi tidak menutup kemungkinan terjadinya perubahan sosial dan politik yang lebih luas, tetapi perubahan tersebut didasarkan pada tindakan awal pembebasan diri ini—perubahan dalam cara kita berhubungan dengan diri sendiri dan orang lain.

Sebagaimana dikatakan Stirner, insureksi memiliki konsekuensi tak terhindarkan berupa transformasi keadaan, “namun tidak dimulai dari keadaan tersebut, melainkan dari ketidakpuasan manusia terhadap dirinya sendiri.” Dengan demikian, insureksi dapat dilihat sebagai bentuk emansipasi diri yang radikal. Insureksi tidak dipandu atau ditentukan oleh pelopor revolusioner atau partai-partai, dan ia tidak berusaha merebut serta mengendalikan kekuasaan negara.

Sebaliknya, ia secara radikal anti-institusional: “Revolusi bertujuan pada pengaturan baru; insureksi membawa kita untuk tidak lagi diatur, tetapi mengatur diri kita sendiri, dan tidak menggantungkan harapan pada ‘institusi’.” Negara tidak dilihat sebagai instrumen transformasi sosial, atau bahkan sebagai hambatan utama kebebasan individu. Insureksi menolak fetisisasi kekuasaan negara ini. Individu egois harus menegaskan dirinya di atas negara; ia tidak lagi melihat negara, baik dalam kekaguman maupun ketakutan (dua sisi mata uang yang sama), melainkan hanya pada dirinya sendiri.

Gagasan unik tentang insureksi ini adalah bagian kunci dari proyek filosofis dan etis egoisme Stirner. Bagi Stirner, di dunia yang penuh dengan “bayangan (spooks)” atau abstraksi ideologis dan ideal-ideal metafisik—seperti kemanusiaan, moralitas, kebebasan, hak, masyarakat, hukum, dan negara—yang merupakan sisa-sisa dari agama namun terus menghantui kita, ego adalah satu-satunya realitas konkret, satu-satunya hal yang nyata dan dapat disentuh.

Politik identitas hanyalah upaya untuk memampatkan “Yang Unik” ke dalam generalisasi fiksi yang mengklaim mewakili esensinya, tetapi pada akhirnya hanya merusak perbedaannya.

Proyek politik, etis, dan filosofis Stirner adalah untuk membebaskan “Yang Unik” dari kepatuhan terhadap abstraksi semacam itu. Ia mendorong kita untuk melihat dunia dan diri kita sendiri dari perspektif kita sendiri serta menolak untuk terpesona oleh “gagasan tetap” dan konsep esensialis apa pun—yaitu, gagasan dan cara hidup yang hanya kita warisi dari tradisi.

Dengan mengadopsi pandangan alternatif “Yang Unik,” segala sesuatu tampak menjadi tidak pasti secara radikal. Dunia terbuka bagi kita. Diri menjadi seperti kanvas kosong yang menunggu untuk diciptakan kembali.

Pendekatan baru terhadap dunia ini memiliki konsekuensi penting dalam hal etika dan politik. Jika dunia menjadi kontingen dan tidak terbatas, maka tindakan tidak lagi dapat didasarkan pada kriteria moral dan rasional yang absolut dan universal. Kita mulai mengenali bahwa kriteria semacam itu sama ilusinya dengan takhayul agama yang mereka gantikan.

Namun, dengan tidak adanya koordinat yang telah ditentukan sebelumnya, kita dipaksa untuk membuat keputusan etis secara independen. Jika kita tidak lagi melihat pada institusi seperti negara atau pada kesamaan seperti bangsa, kita memperoleh sarana untuk menciptakan bentuk organisasi politik dan komunitas yang otonom. Salah satu kemungkinan yang diusulkan Stirner adalah gagasan paradoks tentang “serikat egois” (union of egoists).

Kita sekarang tidak lagi berhubungan dengan orang lain karena kewajiban atau paksaan, tetapi karena hubungan itu membawa kegembiraan atau memperkaya rasa diri kita. Jika bahasa tentang hak dan bahkan kebebasan terasa kabur dan tidak memuaskan, kita dapat menggunakan bahasa alternatif seperti “kepemilikan diri” (ownness) yang memungkinkan kita menentukan jalan kebebasan individu kita sendiri, seunik orang yang menjalaninya.

Insureksi harus dilihat sebagai semacam eksperimen politik dan etika yang dimulai dari diri sendiri dan kemungkinan-kemungkinan pada diri sendiri. Ini adalah ajakan untuk mempraktikkan bentuk-bentuk baru interaksi dan asosiasi yang ditentukan sendiri, serta cara-cara keberadaan baru yang tidak peduli pada kekuasaan.

Anarkis telah memberikan banyak contoh semacam ini, mulai dari praktik sehari-hari seperti menempati bangunan kosong (squatting), menduduki ruang-ruang publik, hingga menciptakan komunitas alternatif secara sadar. Eksperimen-eksperimen ini berpusat pada insureksi di saat ini, di sini dan sekarang, alih-alih menggantungkan harapan pada Event revolusioner besar di masa depan.

Stirner mengajarkan kepada kita bahwa semua politik adalah mikro-politik, bahwa perubahan sosial dan politik dimulai dengan mengubah diri sendiri, melepaskan diri dari kekuasaan, dan mengubah hubungan etis kita dengan orang lain.

Seperti yang pernah dikatakan oleh anarkis Jerman Gustav Landauer, yang sangat terinspirasi oleh Stirner, “Negara adalah hubungan sosial; cara tertentu orang berhubungan satu sama lain. Negara dapat dihancurkan dengan menciptakan hubungan sosial baru, yaitu dengan orang-orang saling berhubungan secara berbeda.”

author: Leanne Sanders
title: Banner message along Edmonton area highway ‘racist’ according to First Nations
content:
The photo of a banner hung from a barbed wire fence along highway 779 northwest of Edmonton went viral after it was posted online over the Heritage Day long weekend. “The Indians have done nothing in 100 years and now they wanna tell us how to run Alberta,” the banner said. It alarmed Kara Burnstick from Alexander First Nation enough that she stopped to take a picture of it. She told APTN News that it feels like attitudes toward First Nations people are getting worse. “A hundred percent. I think that you can definitely sense it, and you can definitely feel it. Just when I’m out, doing grocery shopping or getting gas or something. It’s very unsettling,” said Burnstick said on her social media post. While Burnstick doesn’t know when the banner was placed on the fence, the date of her photo coincided with an “Alberta Independence Walk” and rally by the group Cruise to Alberta Independence in Spruce Grove, south of where the banner was reportedly located. The group has promoted a series of rallies in support of the province separating across Alberta in recent months, ahead of the Oct. 19 referendum. APTN reached out to the group for comment. In an email, “Al Bertan” with the group said they were unaware of the banner. “This is not our approach, so it is definitely not something we would do. But if by chance someone within our community is responsible for [it] I will find out,” they said. The City of Spruce Grove and Sturgeon County were both unaware of the banner. Burnstick, a member of Alexander First Nation said the banner made her do a double take. “I feel very unsafe, and I do feel threatened because this is a neighboring community that’s just outside of our reserve,” Burnstick said. “And, you know, it makes me worrisome for our families and our children and it’s just it’s scary because if they can put the sign up, what else are they capable of?” She said the photo has been shared by thousands of people since she posted it on Saturday. Chris Saulteaux from Paul First Nation said he was so disgusted, he drove to the site and tore the banner down. “When I first saw it, I thought it was probably AI, and then I [saw] it going around more and more on Facebook. And so I don’t know. I just I decided that I was going to go see from my very own eyes that this actually was up and it existed,” Chris Saulteaux said, noting he’s not worried about potential fallout from his actions. Comments on the original photo condemn the use of the banner. “Danielle Smith states that the law will be enforced if First Nations engage in civil disobedience. Yet, the public display of these signs causes severe social, cultural, and safety issues. This is systemic racism and anti-Indigenous racism. It is a public display of hatred and violence driven by entitled separatists,” said Erica Johnson on Facebook. StopHateAB said it’s not only First Nations being impacted by acts such as this. “Sadly, as the referendum in Alberta is approaching anti-Indigenous and hate towards racialized/newcomer communities has been rising in a more public and harmful way, which has been reflected on our online community reporting tool. The political climate has become increasingly volatile and Indigenous communities have been targeted among racialized/newcomer groups in an open and public fashion,” said executive director Nina Saini. “Hateful rhetoric is being encouraged through these despicable public displays and the consequence of political disagreement through this referendum has trickled in to the promotion and emboldened actions promoting racism and discrimination across Alberta. There is no justification for this and the harm being directed towards Indigenous communities, as they stand in unity to remain a united Canada, this type of targeted hate is not acceptable and deeply concerning,” Saini said, adding that StopHateAB “stands in solidarity with the Indigenous peoples and their treaty rights being honored.” The Spruce Grove gathering was part of localized summer rallies—including recent demonstrations in Taber and bridge rallies over Edmonton’s Whitemud Drive. These demonstrations follow a successful citizen initiative petition organized by groups like Stay Free Alberta, which triggered the official fall referendum. The question dealing with separation asks “Should Alberta remain a province of Canada, or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?”Electors may then choose from two options-option 1: Alberta should remain a province of Canada, or option 2 which authorizes the government of Alberta to “commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada. First Nations leaders have been vocal in opposing separation since the Alberta government first moved to amend its Referendum Act to make it easier for a citizen-led petition to make it on a referendum ballot. The change on Dec. 11, 2025 has been viewed as a threat to Treaty rights, including jurisdiction over mineral rights, should the referendum result in a mandate to begin the separation process. APTN reached out to Premier Smith’s office, however, it was the press secretary to Alberta’s Associate Minister of Multiculturalism who responded. “Alberta’s government stands firmly against racism and continues working to build a province where everyone is respected—no matter their cultural background or where they come from. Everyone deserves to feel safe and respected in their communities…,” the statement from Braedyn Funke said in part. However, Deputy Premier Mike Ellis posted a comment on X earlier Tuesday about the right to free speech.

We are committed to supporting and respecting everyone’s right to free speech. We have duty to uphold these rights and freedoms, regardless of an individual’s religious or political beliefs. Alberta’s government does not condone hate speech or violence, but we believe law… — Mike Ellis (@MikeEllisUCP) August 4, 2026

“We are committed to supporting and respecting everyone’s right to free speech,” he wrote. “… but we believe law enforcement should be focused on stopping violent crime, not policing opinions or “hurt feelings,” Ellis’s post said. It’s not clear what Ellis was writing about,  but some comments below were about the banner.

“So being a racist is free speech now?” one commenter said.

“You know “hurt feelings” isn’t the issue,” another said. “That’s a disingenuous talking point. Freedom of expression has legal limits, and enforcing them doesn’t prevent police from tackling violent crime. We can do both. Do better, @MikeEllisUCP —if that’s even possible.”

Saulteaux said Ellis’s post makes him feel like First Nations don’t matter and racism gets “brushed under the under the rug.” Burnstick feels that whoever is responsible for putting up the banner should be held accountable. “If a statement crosses the line into promoting hatred against a protected group, I believe it should be investigated and, where the law applies, prosecuted,” Burnstick said. “We have laws that are meant to protect people from hate speech, and those laws should be applied fairly.” APTN has reached out to Alberta RCMP for comment.

APTN reached out to Premier Smith’s office, however, it was the press secretary to Alberta’s Associate Minister of Multiculturalism who responded. “Alberta’s government stands firmly against racism and continues working to build a province where everyone is respected—no matter their cultural background or where they come from. Everyone deserves to feel safe and respected in their communities…,” the statement from Braedyn Funke said in part. However, Deputy Premier Mike Ellis posted a comment on X earlier Tuesday about the right to free speech.

We are committed to supporting and respecting everyone’s right to free speech. We have duty to uphold these rights and freedoms, regardless of an individual’s religious or political beliefs. Alberta’s government does not condone hate speech or violence, but we believe law… — Mike Ellis (@MikeEllisUCP) August 4, 2026

“We are committed to supporting and respecting everyone’s right to free speech,” he wrote. “… but we believe law enforcement should be focused on stopping violent crime, not policing opinions or “hurt feelings,” Ellis’s post said. It’s not clear what Ellis was writing about,  but some comments below were about the banner.
“So being a racist is free speech now?” one commenter said.

title: Gjoa Haven boil water advisory lifted after months-long disruption
content:
Gjoa Haven residents can now drink tap water without boiling it first, after the Department of Health lifted the community’s boil water advisory, which was in place for nearly seven months.

Last Friday, the Government of Nunavut received two consecutive bacteriological samples for Gjoa Haven, said health department spokesperson Charmaine Deogracias in an interview.

Both tested negative for fecal coliform and total coliform — bacteria that can indicate contamination from human or animal waste.

Regional environmental health officer Sharlene Lively reviewed the results, Deogracias said.

The Department of Health then recommended that the advisory be lifted, with final approval coming from Nunavut Chief Public Health Officer Dr. Ekua Agyemang.

The advisory had been in place since Jan. 16, after a break was discovered in a six-kilometre water main that connected Swan Lake to the community’s water treatment plant.

Although the Hamlet of Gjoa Haven completed repairs to restore the water supply on June 17, the advisory remained in place while Nunavut’s Department of Transportation and Infrastructure cleaned and disinfected the water storage tank.

The tank was flushed on July 24, the department said in an emailed update. The delay was due to scheduling qualified tradespeople, it said.

title: After More Than 20 Years in Prison, Georgia Man Wins New Trial in “Shaken Baby” Case
content:
A Georgia court has ordered a new trial for Danyel Smith, a father who was convicted of killing his two-month-old son, Chandler, more than twenty years ago. Prosecutors relied on a diagnosis of Shaken Baby Syndrome (SBS) to secure his conviction. In recent years, scientific evidence has emerged calling into question the basic assumptions behind the hypothesis.

In her decision, Gwinnett County Superior Court Judge Kimberly A. Gallant ruled that the evolving research into SBS, also known as Abusive Head Trauma (AHT), constitutes new evidence that was not known at the time of trial.

“Mr. Smith’s evidence is not based on historical facts or eyewitness testimony, but on expert analysis grounded in the application of evolving scientific knowledge,” Gallant wrote in her decision .

Medical experts for the defense have concluded that Chandler was not the victim of abuse.

The defense experts surmise that on the day he fell unconscious, he had a seizure, went into respiratory distress, and stopped breathing. This was at least the second seizure Chandler, who was born five-weeks premature, had experienced, according to Smith’s legal filings. When he was less than two weeks old his mother called 911 and reported that he was breathing strangely and appeared to be having a seizure. The responding paramedics dismissed her concerns. (Smith was not home at the time.)

The expert opinions underlying his motion for a new trial, the judge wrote, “are informed by research advancements in medicine, scientific developments, peer-reviewed literature, and evolving medical standards.”

At the time of Smith’s trial, there was largely a consensus among the scientific and legal communities about the veracity of SBS/AHT. But in the decades since, exonerations and studies have revealed that the so-called triad of symptoms associated with SBS/AHT—bleeding around the eyes, bleeding between the skull and brain, and brain swelling—can be caused by strokes, short-distance falls, childbirth trauma, and disease.

What was once considered to be virtually unassailable evidence of abuse is now, in the words of one New Jersey judge , increasingly understood to be “akin to ‘junk science.’”

On April 29, 2002, Smith was driving his eight-week-old son, Chandler, to a benefits office so that his partner could apply for food assistance. On the ride over, Smith looked at Chandler when he was stopped at a red light and saw that he was pale and not breathing, according to Smith’s motion for a new trial. Smith’s petition says that in a “frantic phone call” he told his partner that something was wrong with the baby and drove to where she was waiting.

He carried the baby out of the car and Chandler’s mother called 911. Bystanders attempted to perform CPR. When the paramedics arrived, they took Chandler to the hospital.

The next day, a child abuse specialist examined Chandler and concluded that he had been shaken. On May 1, Smith was arrested at the hospital. Less than a week later, his son was taken off life support and died.

“[T]here’s no other explanation that the doctors might look for that would explain these symptoms, other than non-accidental trauma, that is, child abuse,” the prosecutor told the jury during opening arguments at Smith’s trial.

The county medical examiner testified that Chandler’s injuries “are classic and in some cases virtually exclusive for violent shaking.”

Smith maintained his innocence.

“I did not shake my son,” Smith told the jury.

On November 21, 2003, Smith was convicted of felony murder, cruelty to children, and aggravated battery. The judge sentenced him to life in prison.

Smith has never stopped trying to prove his innocence. In 2021, the Southern Center for Human Rights took up his case and began an exhaustive investigation.

In 2021, Smith’s attorneys filed a petition for a new trial, but did not receive an evidentiary hearing until 2024. Prior to the hearing, the Gwinnett County prosecutor’s office offered Smith a plea deal . In exchange for pleading guilty, he would get time served and be released from prison, according to Smith’s legal filings. Smith rejected it.

“He’s now served 24 years in prison, that’s half of his life,” Smith’s attorney, Mark Loudon-Brown, told The Appeal. “During that time, he turned down the opportunity to go home simply because he refused to admit to a crime he did not commit.”

At his evidentiary hearing, held in 2024, numerous specialists testified for the defense, but the court denied Smith’s petition ruling that “almost twenty years of advancement in medical science has not undermined the conclusions reached at the Defendant’s trial.”

The Supreme Court of Georgia reversed the lower court’s denial and sent the case back down to the Superior Court of Gwinnett County. While the case was on appeal, the judge who had denied Smith’s petition retired.

In Judge Gallant’s ruling she wrote that since Smith’s conviction, there had been a “fundamental shift in the diagnostic approach to brain findings in infants.” SBS/AHT was no longer treated as a “presumptive diagnosis.”

“[C]urrent medical and scientific standards require a comprehensive differential diagnosis that considers alternative, non-abusive causes before concluding abuse,” she wrote.

Smith has presented “an alternative medical explanation for Chandler’s death that is so material that it would probably produce a different verdict,” Gallant concluded. This explanation is “corroborated by five medical specialists, including three pathologists, a radiologist, and a pediatric neurosurgeon.”

The next steps for the case are “largely in the prosecution’s hands,” said Loudon-Brown. They could appeal the judge’s decision, retry the case, or dismiss it, he said.

The prosecutor’s office has not yet said how they plan to proceed and declined to comment when contacted by The Appeal.

Smith’s legal team has filed a motion for bond, which, if granted, would allow him to come home while his case is pending before the court. Loudon-Brown told The Appeal that they had asked the prosecutor’s office to consent to a bond, but they refused. In Smith’s motion, his attorneys note that the prosecutors’ previous plea offer of time served shows “that the District Attorney is comfortable with Mr. Smith returning to the community.” Their motion also notes that Smith has no other convictions and has never received a disciplinary report during his more than twenty years of incarceration.

A hearing on Smith’s bond motion is scheduled for September.

Smith’s years-long battle to prove his innocence is par for the course for wrongfully convicted people, especially those accused of crimes that never occurred.

“DNA evidence is very helpful in reversing a conviction because it’s showing it’s not one person who did it, it’s another person,” attorney Valena Beety recently told The Appeal . But if there was no crime, “there was no perpetrator,” which means DNA evidence can’t help exonerate the wrongfully convicted person.

As a result, many people convicted in SBS/AHT cases continue to struggle to have their cases re-examined.

In Mississippi, Beety’s client, Tasha Shelby , is still incarcerated for a crime that likely never occurred. In 2000, a jury convicted Shelby of capital murder for shaking to death her fiancé’s two-year-old son. Almost twenty years later, the medical examiner who had ruled the boy’s death a homicide testified at an evidentiary hearing that he now believed the child had fallen and suffered a seizure, and that the child’s asthma had also contributed to his death. Appeals courts have nonetheless upheld her conviction.

In Texas, Robert Roberson remains on death row for shaking his two-year-old daughter to death despite evidence that suggests she died from a severe case of viral and bacterial pneumonia. The former lead detective on Roberson’s case, Brian Wharton , is now one of his most outspoken supporters.

“It’s not simply stopping an execution,” Wharton told The Appeal in 2024. “We owe it to him to say, ‘Yes, Robert’ — call him by name — ‘Robert, you are correct. You are right. We were wrong.’ And set him free.”

However, some courts are finally taking a more critical look at these cases. Forty-three people have been exonerated in SBS/AHT cases, according to the National Registry of Exonerations . About 83 percent of those occurred since Smith’s conviction.

Last year, in a groundbreaking decision, the New Jersey Supreme Court banned testimony on SBS from the state’s courtrooms, ruling that “there is no general acceptance in the biomechanical community of the SBS/AHT without impact diagnosis.”

Smith’s attorney, Loudon-Brown, says courts are beginning to correct some of the mistakes of the past.

“More and more courts are recognizing that science changes, science evolves,” he told The Appeal. “Sometimes those advances in science allow for new evidence that undermines convictions that were based on outdated science. All you have to do is just apply the law.”

title: Anarchists in the Tenant Movement #3 – the Southeast
content:
This is the third installment of our Anarchists in the Tenant Movement series. You can find the first installment here and the second here . The interview below was conducted with an organizer named Mario, involved in a tenant union in the US Southeast. We’ve concealed Mario’s specific location at his request.

Like our other series Anarchists in the Labor Movement , these interviews aim to capture insights and perspectives from anarchists who are active in tenant organizing. Some of those we speak to are organizing through established tenant unions, others are building new unions, while others still are launching initial campaigns without a formal union yet.

For Black Rose / Rosa Negra (BRRN), mass organizations like tenant unions play a central role in our strategy . It’s through these kinds of organizations that people create and apply their collective leverage against structures that dominate and exploit us, such as landlordism and private property. By engaging consistently in everyday campaigns members of mass organizations grow their collective confidence and power, enabling them to take on ever bigger fights and ultimately to challenge the very existence of these dominating structures.

In part, the aim of this series is simply to shine a spotlight on the presence of anarchist militants in the U.S. tenant movement. More substantively, we ask participants to critically reflect on their experiences, including both successes and failures, to draw out generalizable lessons.

Most, but not all of those interviewed in this series are members of BRRN.

Answers have been edited for clarity and length.

Mario – Tenant Organizer in the Southeast

Black Rose/Rosa Negra (BRRN): How would you summarize your political beliefs in one sentence?

Mario: I want all people to have autonomy, self determination, and the opportunity to reach their full potential, and I think that’s only achievable through a collective liberation from capitalism, the state, and the social hierarchy that props them up. One sentence is tough!

BRRN: Prior to tenant organizing, did you have any other organizing experience?

Mario: I had done some political activism but nothing that involved convincing people who weren’t already interested in the project to take action or organize together. I started from the direction of organizing for the advancement of black people, mainly with education and things like voter registration drives. I participated in the George Floyd uprisings, and got into anti-policing efforts after that. I also did some mutual aid work, or what’s commonly known as mutual aid (but feels mostly like charity). Both experiences taught me that activists showing up week after week to protest or volunteer doesn’t always transmit to change, and that power doesn’t necessarily flow from large public pressure.

If the only place you interact with people that need aid is at the distro, they continue to only be served at the distro – I noticed often that the people being served were rarely making real decisions or holding power in any way. The closest they got was something like an exit survey asking whether the aid provided was what they needed. I had to step back and process all of it and ended up learning about the tenant union.

I started to research tenant unionism because I’d been interested in labor unions but had never been in a traditionally unionized industry or had a job that felt right to try to unionize, but I’d had plenty of difficulty in tenancy and it seemed like somewhere I could actually do the “mutual” part of mutual aid. The funny thing is that I had participated in multiple walkouts and labor actions that took place outside of a union structure without ever realizing what they were, what they meant or the possibilities that those ruptures could’ve opened up. Even in answering this, I’m just now remembering that they were probably the most militant forms of organizing I’ve engaged in so far.

BRRN: What tenant union are you part of, and about how many people are part of it?

Mario: I’m a member of a tenant union in a mid-sized metro area in the southeast US. We have about 70 dues paying members right now, with a couple of building-level tenant associations.

BRRN: How is your tenant union organized?

Mario: It’s organized into city-based locals made up of building-level tenant associations and at-large members. The locals meet to support each others’ organizing and plan day-to-day activities of the union and make decisions regarding where to spend our time and energy. Members of the locals plus at-large members in the county make up the whole union, and each of these levels makes its decisions in a direct democracy of members.

There are also union-wide committees that carry out essential functions for the growth and development of the union (e.g. an organizing committee), with elected chairs. The elected chairs sit on a committee tasked with putting on the general body meetings and carrying out the proposals or resolutions that are adopted at the general meetings, as well as coordinating across the committees and addressing significant union-wide challenges.

BRRN: What are some of the things you do as a tenant organizer?

Mario: I canvass, have one on ones with neighbors and tenants at complexes we’re helping to organize, give organizing trainings, organize solidarity support for unions and local organizations, and table to find new members and organizing leads. I research and study to find weak points of the local landlords and the municipal structure, as well as learning strategies other tenant unions are using. I also attend and help set up our local meetings and participate in committee and general meetings. Oh, and potlucks: food is part of a lot of our in-person meetings and we’ll have a social every couple months.

BRRN: Describe a campaign you are currently or were most recently involved in: how did it start, what are the main issues, what strategy and tactics are being used?

Mario: We’re starting a campaign against a non-profit landlord. It began when one of their tenants came to a local meeting and started organizing their building, and then another one came and both building organizing drives kicked off. They’ve had some success with just their buildings, so now they are hoping to establish a campaign across all the buildings. The main issues are ignored maintenance and accommodations requests, security and safety issues around building access, and threats of eviction by management. Tactics being used now include petitions and public pressure, but there are planned escalations depending on the results.

BRRN: What resources have helped you the most in developing as a tenant organizer?

Mario: The Madrid Tenants’ Union organizing handbook is a very solid base. It includes everything from how to canvass, run meetings, and escalate a campaign with a lot of insights on how to organize. The Autonomous Tenant Union Network’s “kitchen table sessions,” where organizers from different tenant unions across the country can learn from each other, were great for learning on the ground strategy lessons and connecting with tenant unions organizing under similar conditions. Most of what comes out of Labor Notes is applicable to tenant organizing as well.

BRRN: How do your anarchist politics relate to/inform the day-to-day of tenant organizing work?

Mario: The main way it shows up is in how I view the organizing process. I want wins for tenants, but I want it to actually be the tenants winning. I think this is a common perspective among a lot of people in the tenant movement but it comes out in different ways. To me, it’s about showing up to support and building people up to be the protagonist in their own struggle. It’s being a co-equal participant and not a “community organizer.” It’s sharing knowledge and effort to help people learn to facilitate their own meetings, plan their own actions, and run their own fights. But it’s also fighting in places that aren’t just good targets for organizing, and a belief that I should be struggling forward as well and not just convincing others to do so, in whatever fashion is necessary for those specific conditions.

It also informs the way I approach the union generally. The union began as a project of external organizers, and it really heavily shaped the early character of the organization. In a lot of ways we’ve moved past that, but in others it’s still very present – It’s squarely a leftist organization so I don’t worry too much about us deviating from focusing on the class interests of tenants, but I do worry about where our energy gets focused, how we make decisions and who they are made by, and the distribution of both labor and knowledge within the union.

BRRN: How do tenant unions fit into a broader strategy aimed at revolutionary social transformation?

Mario: When I think about the things that have to change as we build toward social revolution, the first thing that comes up is the fight/flight/freeze stress response. The general responses from tenants seem to be freeze or flight, in that people are mostly accepting the conditions and trying to float or they’re leaving for better conditions. It’s a very common response by tenants: “I’ll just move somewhere else next year.” People don’t know any other way right now, so it’s necessary to develop combative formations to show people that fighting is actually an option, and to show them that they have power and can win those fights.

Tenant unions are a formation where ordinary people can learn and practice class struggle and solidarity. Forming a tenant union and demanding improvements to your conditions either shows people their agency and power or gives them a fight. It helps people make connections between their own experience and struggles and the general economic and political system, and really lays bare the class contradictions between landlords, property management, real estate developers, and the rest of us. In the past week, I’ve heard two tenants ask why the property management neglects tenants and their apartment complexes and then describe what they would do with the place if they were running it. Having a real say in the circumstances of your life and engaging in the struggle to win that say can change the character of people and spur a desire for greater control and agency.

There is also an aspect of prefiguration to tenant organizing, depending on how it’s done. If you build democracy into the union, if you’re running your own fights, solving your own conflicts and developing the knowledge and ability needed for self management, you’re building your revolutionary capacity. If there’s ever going to be a successful transfer of control over housing and land to the people, not only will having these structures in place be necessary to handle management and control of social production, but people will need to be comfortable operating within them.

BRRN: What advice would you share with anarchists looking to organize or become active in a tenant union? What do you wish you had known when you started?

Mario: It depends on if they’re new to organizing generally. If so, I would say to focus on the the concrete tasks of organizing tenants. It’s easy to get caught up in setting up the most ideal system and support projects for the union and miss that the only people in it are the people you started with. There is a lot of information and theory on the best way to carry out “organizing” and building solidarity and confidence for fighting the landlords, but don’t just blindly follow those guides. Commit to a strategy and then bring together the people you tried it with to seriously reflect on its efficacy. Do this even with individual conversations – not in the way of just second guessing yourself, but asking why things you said did or didn’t move the person you were talking to. I wasted a lot of time early on just following the training, failing, and then applying the same training with refined execution, instead of assessing whether the execution or the training was the issue.

For the more experienced organizer, I’d say there is a lot of political interest in tenant unions right now, for better or worse, and so you do need to be aware of the local political ecosystem and how your union interacts with it. It can have a significant impact on the direction of the union, which brings up a second point around small formations vs. established unions. When the union is small, it’s a lot easier to get scooped up in a larger organization’s presence or influence, but it also makes it easier to build in some defenses against that and to build a culture in the union that prioritizes tenant power. It can be a lot to work with, so don’t try to take it all on yourself: your neighbors and the other people in your union are all facing the same issues as you and you can build up trust and shared understanding of what needs to be done that will protect you all as you go on.

contentBlocks.text: This is the third installment of our Anarchists in the Tenant Movement series. You can find the first installment here and the second here. The interview below was conducted with an organizer named Mario, involved in a tenant union in the US Southeast. We’ve concealed Mario’s specific location at his request.

Like our other series Anarchists in the Labor Movement, these interviews aim to capture insights and perspectives from anarchists who are active in tenant organizing. Some of those we speak to are organizing through established tenant unions, others are building new unions, while others still are launching initial campaigns without a formal union yet.

For Black Rose / Rosa Negra (BRRN), mass organizations like tenant unions play a central role in our strategy. It’s through these kinds of organizations that people create and apply their collective leverage against structures that dominate and exploit us, such as landlordism and private property. By engaging consistently in everyday campaigns members of mass organizations grow their collective confidence and power, enabling them to take on ever bigger fights and ultimately to challenge the very existence of these dominating structures.

In part, the aim of this series is simply to shine a spotlight on the presence of anarchist militants in the U.S. tenant movement. More substantively, we ask participants to critically reflect on their experiences, including both successes and failures, to draw out generalizable lessons.
Most, but not all of those interviewed in this series are members of BRRN.
Answers have been edited for clarity and length.
Mario – Tenant Organizer in the Southeast
Black Rose/Rosa Negra (BRRN): How would you summarize your political beliefs in one sentence?

Mario: I want all people to have autonomy, self determination, and the opportunity to reach their full potential, and I think that’s only achievable through a collective liberation from capitalism, the state, and the social hierarchy that props them up. One sentence is tough!
BRRN: Prior to tenant organizing, did you have any other organizing experience?

Mario: I had done some political activism but nothing that involved convincing people who weren’t already interested in the project to take action or organize together. I started from the direction of organizing for the advancement of black people, mainly with education and things like voter registration drives. I participated in the George Floyd uprisings, and got into anti-policing efforts after that. I also did some mutual aid work, or what’s commonly known as mutual aid (but feels mostly like charity). Both experiences taught me that activists showing up week after week to protest or volunteer doesn’t always transmit to change, and that power doesn’t necessarily flow from large public pressure.

If the only place you interact with people that need aid is at the distro, they continue to only be served at the distro – I noticed often that the people being served were rarely making real decisions or holding power in any way. The closest they got was something like an exit survey asking whether the aid provided was what they needed. I had to step back and process all of it and ended up learning about the tenant union.

I started to research tenant unionism because I’d been interested in labor unions but had never been in a traditionally unionized industry or had a job that felt right to try to unionize, but I’d had plenty of difficulty in tenancy and it seemed like somewhere I could actually do the “mutual” part of mutual aid. The funny thing is that I had participated in multiple walkouts and labor actions that took place outside of a union structure without ever realizing what they were, what they meant or the possibilities that those ruptures could’ve opened up. Even in answering this, I’m just now remembering that they were probably the most militant forms of organizing I’ve engaged in so far.
BRRN: What tenant union are you part of, and about how many people are part of it?
Mario: I’m a member of a tenant union in a mid-sized metro area in the southeast US. We have about 70 dues paying members right now, with a couple of building-level tenant associations.
BRRN: How is your tenant union organized?

Mario: It’s organized into city-based locals made up of building-level tenant associations and at-large members. The locals meet to support each others’ organizing and plan day-to-day activities of the union and make decisions regarding where to spend our time and energy. Members of the locals plus at-large members in the county make up the whole union, and each of these levels makes its decisions in a direct democracy of members.

There are also union-wide committees that carry out essential functions for the growth and development of the union (e.g. an organizing committee), with elected chairs. The elected chairs sit on a committee tasked with putting on the general body meetings and carrying out the proposals or resolutions that are adopted at the general meetings, as well as coordinating across the committees and addressing significant union-wide challenges.
BRRN: What are some of the things you do as a tenant organizer?

Mario: I canvass, have one on ones with neighbors and tenants at complexes we’re helping to organize, give organizing trainings, organize solidarity support for unions and local organizations, and table to find new members and organizing leads. I research and study to find weak points of the local landlords and the municipal structure, as well as learning strategies other tenant unions are using. I also attend and help set up our local meetings and participate in committee and general meetings. Oh, and potlucks: food is part of a lot of our in-person meetings and we’ll have a social every couple months.
BRRN: Describe a campaign you are currently or were most recently involved in: how did it start, what are the main issues, what strategy and tactics are being used?

Mario: We’re starting a campaign against a non-profit landlord. It began when one of their tenants came to a local meeting and started organizing their building, and then another one came and both building organizing drives kicked off. They’ve had some success with just their buildings, so now they are hoping to establish a campaign across all the buildings. The main issues are ignored maintenance and accommodations requests, security and safety issues around building access, and threats of eviction by management. Tactics being used now include petitions and public pressure, but there are planned escalations depending on the results.
BRRN: What resources have helped you the most in developing as a tenant organizer?

Mario: The Madrid Tenants’ Union organizing handbook is a very solid base. It includes everything from how to canvass, run meetings, and escalate a campaign with a lot of insights on how to organize. The Autonomous Tenant Union Network’s “kitchen table sessions,” where organizers from different tenant unions across the country can learn from each other, were great for learning on the ground strategy lessons and connecting with tenant unions organizing under similar conditions. Most of what comes out of Labor Notes is applicable to tenant organizing as well.
BRRN: How do your anarchist politics relate to/inform the day-to-day of tenant organizing work?

Mario: The main way it shows up is in how I view the organizing process. I want wins for tenants, but I want it to actually be the tenants winning. I think this is a common perspective among a lot of people in the tenant movement but it comes out in different ways. To me, it’s about showing up to support and building people up to be the protagonist in their own struggle. It’s being a co-equal participant and not a “community organizer.” It’s sharing knowledge and effort to help people learn to facilitate their own meetings, plan their own actions, and run their own fights. But it’s also fighting in places that aren’t just good targets for organizing, and a belief that I should be struggling forward as well and not just convincing others to do so, in whatever fashion is necessary for those specific conditions.

It also informs the way I approach the union generally. The union began as a project of external organizers, and it really heavily shaped the early character of the organization. In a lot of ways we’ve moved past that, but in others it’s still very present – It’s squarely a leftist organization so I don’t worry too much about us deviating from focusing on the class interests of tenants, but I do worry about where our energy gets focused, how we make decisions and who they are made by, and the distribution of both labor and knowledge within the union.
BRRN: How do tenant unions fit into a broader strategy aimed at revolutionary social transformation?

Mario: When I think about the things that have to change as we build toward social revolution, the first thing that comes up is the fight/flight/freeze stress response. The general responses from tenants seem to be freeze or flight, in that people are mostly accepting the conditions and trying to float or they’re leaving for better conditions. It’s a very common response by tenants: “I’ll just move somewhere else next year.” People don’t know any other way right now, so it’s necessary to develop combative formations to show people that fighting is actually an option, and to show them that they have power and can win those fights.

Tenant unions are a formation where ordinary people can learn and practice class struggle and solidarity. Forming a tenant union and demanding improvements to your conditions either shows people their agency and power or gives them a fight. It helps people make connections between their own experience and struggles and the general economic and political system, and really lays bare the class contradictions between landlords, property management, real estate developers, and the rest of us. In the past week, I’ve heard two tenants ask why the property management neglects tenants and their apartment complexes and then describe what they would do with the place if they were running it. Having a real say in the circumstances of your life and engaging in the struggle to win that say can change the character of people and spur a desire for greater control and agency.

There is also an aspect of prefiguration to tenant organizing, depending on how it’s done. If you build democracy into the union, if you’re running your own fights, solving your own conflicts and developing the knowledge and ability needed for self management, you’re building your revolutionary capacity. If there’s ever going to be a successful transfer of control over housing and land to the people, not only will having these structures in place be necessary to handle management and control of social production, but people will need to be comfortable operating within them.
BRRN: What advice would you share with anarchists looking to organize or become active in a tenant union? What do you wish you had known when you started?

Mario: It depends on if they’re new to organizing generally. If so, I would say to focus on the the concrete tasks of organizing tenants. It’s easy to get caught up in setting up the most ideal system and support projects for the union and miss that the only people in it are the people you started with. There is a lot of information and theory on the best way to carry out “organizing” and building solidarity and confidence for fighting the landlords, but don’t just blindly follow those guides. Commit to a strategy and then bring together the people you tried it with to seriously reflect on its efficacy. Do this even with individual conversations – not in the way of just second guessing yourself, but asking why things you said did or didn’t move the person you were talking to. I wasted a lot of time early on just following the training, failing, and then applying the same training with refined execution, instead of assessing whether the execution or the training was the issue.

For the more experienced organizer, I’d say there is a lot of political interest in tenant unions right now, for better or worse, and so you do need to be aware of the local political ecosystem and how your union interacts with it. It can have a significant impact on the direction of the union, which brings up a second point around small formations vs. established unions. When the union is small, it’s a lot easier to get scooped up in a larger organization’s presence or influence, but it also makes it easier to build in some defenses against that and to build a culture in the union that prioritizes tenant power. It can be a lot to work with, so don’t try to take it all on yourself: your neighbors and the other people in your union are all facing the same issues as you and you can build up trust and shared understanding of what needs to be done that will protect you all as you go on.

title: Indigenous people demand more say at the UN, as new crises hit their homelands
content:
A Mapuche woman sings as part of closing ceremonies of the United Nations Expert Mechanism on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (EMRIP) in Geneva this week, as the body’s expert panelists sit behind her. She told the assembly, ‘For all who work with all the strength of Mother Earth … let us be united with a single heart.’ 

Photo by Dionne Phillips




This story is published through the Indigenous News Alliance.







In Sápmi (northern Scandinavia), the Arctic is experiencing warming temperatures four times faster than other regions, disproportionately hurting the livelihoods and culture of the Sámi people — particularly their access to vital traditional natural resources such as reindeer and salmon.




As temperatures warm, for example, snow is melting then refreezing at an accelerating rate — forming ice that prevents reindeer from reaching their food supply underneath. More and more of the species are 

starving

 as a result.




“Those impacts in nature are severe for our culture and livelihoods,” said Tuomas Aslak Juuso, vice-president of the 

Sámediggi

 (Sámi Parliament) of “Finland,” in an interview.







READ MORE:

 

Indigenous leaders confront overlapping crises at UN, as climate and conflict collide







The Sámi are the only officially recognized Indigenous people in the European Union.




Their population, estimated between 80,000 and 100,000 people, spans “Norway,” “Finland,” “Sweden” and “Russia.”




Juuso — who was previously his parliament’s elected president — also 

sits

 on the 

Sámiráđđi (Saami Council)

, a body of 15 delegates from Sámi organizations in all four countries. 




Sámi parliaments also co-ordinate across borders through the 

Sámi Parliamentary Council

.




Caribou across the world’s Arctic region are severely impacted by climate change. 

Photo by Morgan Anderson/Parks Canada




A recent 

report

 by the Finnish Meteorological Institute highlights warming winters and fewer months with permanent snow cover, with more and more snow days replaced with rain.




“So survival of reindeer and then survival of our livelihoods [and] cultures is then questioned,” Juuso said, during meetings of the United Nations Expert Mechanism on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (EMRIP) in Geneva last week.




Reindeer are a particularly important species to his people, he explained; along with the animal husbandry, the ungulates are also used for handicrafts including clothing and weapons.







READ MORE:

 

Indigenous peoples bear the brunt of climate change — but get almost none of the money to fight it







Hundreds of Indigenous people gathered at the UN’s headquarters in Geneva for EMRIP’s annual meetings.




They discussed everything from the climate change to continued colonialism, and other issues impacting their homeland.




But one common thread throughout the gathering — and across hundreds of cultures represented there — was the unified demand for a greater voice in international negotiations and decision-making.




Hundreds of delegates represented states, non-government organizations, and Indigenous groups at the United Nations EMRIP meetings in Geneva over the last week. 

Photo by Dionne Phillips




International forum essential, but barriers remain




At EMRIP’s 19th session, delegates discussed what changes they felt are needed to ensure UN member states respect Indigenous people’s rights, land and cultures — in hopes of issuing recommendations on improving human rights protections.




On Wednesday, attendees took part in a session titled “Enhancing the participation of Indigenous Peoples in the United Nations.”




For the Sámi people, having the opportunity to discuss these issues on the international stage is essential, Juuso said — but there are still barriers to their ability to participate. 




Multiple delegates at the meetings accused their states of prioritizing economic growth and development at the expense of land degradation. 




A new 

study

 in 

Ecological Economics

 journal — based on surveys of nearly 160,000 people in 92 countries — found three-in-five favour environmental protection over economic growth.







READ MORE:

 

As disasters worsen, Indigenous peoples threatened by a ‘crisis communication gap’







Having Indigenous voices heard internationally benefits all humanity, many EMRIP delegates emphasized — especially since the body’s recommendations are provided directly to UN member states.  




Speaking out collectively, and showing mutual solidarity across similar struggles, underscores the importance of Indigenous Peoples’ efforts for self-determination and defending their territories, delegates said.




“There’s a real sense of solidarity and common purpose,” said Kym Hamilton, from the iwi (Māori nations) of Ngāti Kahungunu, Ngā Rauru, and Ngāti Raukawa in Aotearoa (New Zealand).




For nearly a decade, she has been involved with the 

Aotearoa Independent Monitoring Mechanism

 for UNDRIP — a group whose members are nominated by their iwi.




“At EMRIP, there’s a lot more opportunity, I think, to meet and engage and collectivize,” she said. 










Kym Hamilton, from the iwi (Māori nations) of Ngāti Kahungunu, Ngā Rauru, and Ngāti Raukawa in Aotearoa (New Zealand). 

Photo by Dionne Phillips




The Government of New Zealand’s delegates to EMRIP. 

Photo by Dionne Phillips










Colonial nation-states dominate UN




One of the biggest barriers identified is restrictions on who can take part in UN events — even those directly dealing with tribal issues and concerns — such as the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP) and the UN Human Rights Council, which oversees EMRIP. 




Member states are automatically granted access to UN gatherings, and can easily express their views, and explain their progress on implementing their international commitments under UNDRIP and other agreements. 




But Indigenous advocates say the voices of the peoples directly involved are seldom heard at international forums. 




The current UN structure requires participation through either a member state, or a registered civil society agency — for instance a non-governmental organization (NGO), academic institution, or accredited Indigenous organization. 




For some Indigenous peoples hoping to attend such high-profile forums, this does not always encompass all the ways they organize themselves.




Agencies like EMRIP can advise states on strengthening human rights and Indigenous voices. 




They also offer a platform for communicating and collaborating between member states and Indigenous peoples, as they confront emerging challenges such as 

artificial intelligence

, 

climate emergencies

, and 

conflict

.







READ MORE:

 

For Indigenous peoples worldwide, conflict means much more than war







“What we are trying to do is to get some implementation resources for us to adapt to the climate change,” Juuso said.




“With Finland, for example, we don’t have any adaptation resources on how to adapt to these situations.”




But to collectively tackle such challenges impacting Indigenous people everywhere, he notes, the UN’s accreditation process can be a stumbling block — including who it allows to officially take part.




“To be able to bring these issues forward to the global discussion, we would have to have the opportunity to participate,” he added.




“For us, as a representative institution, there isn’t actually any clear path to accreditate ourselves — and that leads to them trying to improvise, and try to find ways how we can accreditate ourselves.”




Hundreds of Indigenous organization delegates attend the UN EMRIP meetings in Geneva last week. 

Photo by Dionne Phillips




Enhancing Indigenous participation




In UN lexicon, “

enhanced participation

” is a catchphrase often used to describe efforts to elevate Indigenous Peoples’ voices in an international body otherwise dominated by states.




As part of a decades-long push for a seat at the table, delegates to EMRIP asserted the right to represent their own Indigenous communities in crucial global discussions impacting them. 




They are also demanding more respect from member-state governments and other policy-makers, which they argue will better help them to survive conflict and other crises.




At this year’s meetings, Hamilton delivered an intervention statement on behalf of the National Iwi Chairs Forum, which represents 87 Māori nations.




Hamilton was one of the many delegates who spoke on the agenda item, and offered recommendations to enact the resolutions already on the international table, particularly the UN Human Rights Council, which established EMRIP in 2007.




“The question before us is no longer whether Indigenous peoples should participate more fully in the Human Rights Council,” Hamilton argued in her intervention. 




“The question now is how quickly we will implement these commitments.” 







READ MORE:

 

AI data centers are booming. Indigenous People want help protecting their lands and knowledge







Her recommendations to EMRIP’S expert members included setting a clear timeline on a resolution to create a new official status for Indigenous organizations to participate in UN proceedings, and appointing Indigenous and state co-facilitators with equal standing to lead the process.




She also urged the establishment of an independent and transparent accreditation mechanism, to prevent states from vetoing Indigenous representatives, and the voluntary fund and other initiatives to provide predictable and sustainable funding to take part.




In an interview, Hamilton said Indigenous Peoples must be allowed to participate fully in international deliberations, but that they have the right to decide who represents their communities themselves — not states.




“Governments don’t always tell the truth,” she said, citing the UN Human Rights Council’s 

Universal Periodic Review

 — which every member state must undergo every 4.5 years — which she said showed gaps between the reports governments submitted and the actual human rights situation within their jurisdictions.




She said direct Indigenous nations’ representation is essential, because Indigenous rights are “collective rights around our language, our culture, our land,” she said, different from other human rights she said are “individual rights.”




“We’re meant to be the United Nations,” she added. 




“We’re meant to unite nations, and we recognize ourselves as nations. We are not organizations.”




Kenneth Deer, from the Mohawk Nation at Kahnawà:ke, stands in the halls of the United Nations in Geneva, where he has spoken out for Indigenous rights for decades. 

Photo by Dionne Phillips




This point was echoed by Kenneth Deer, a member of the Mohawk Nation at Kahnawà:ke and longtime UN advocate.




“The government never speaks ill about itself,” he said in an interview. 




“You can’t let government speak for us.”




The National Congress of American Indians (NCAI) also gave recommendations to EMRIP, in a 

statement demanding increased accommodation

 for Indigenous people to take part.







READ MORE:

 

At the UN, Mohawk leader calls for UNDRIP watchdogs to ensure standards are met







“Recognition and participation of Indigenous peoples must accommodate the numerous ways we identify, organize, and represent ourselves,” said NCAI’S president Mark Macarro, who also serves as Tribal Chairman of the Pechanga Band of Indians in “California.”




“It is essential that we participate directly in matters of global concern that affect our environment, health, human rights, and unique rights as Indigenous peoples.”




Their action items include measures already outlined in previous reports, and providing all technical, financial, and human resources needed to expand Indigenous People’s participation.




Leading up to EMRIP’s 19th session this week, participants — including representatives from states, Indigenous Peoples’ Organizations, and NGOs prepared what they called a “

zero draft

” discussing ways to increase Indigenous participation at UN sessions.




Rapid changes ‘on the frontlines’ 




Delegates speaking at the meetings also identified other barriers to meaningful international participation.




For example, communications technology within remote communities presents challenges to joining global deliberations. 




Additionally, there are significant financial barriers for under-resourced communities when UN forums are held far from their homelands.




And as delegations travel from different countries, a lack of co-ordination can sometimes lead to “competing interests” in discussions, Hamilton noted.




Several attendees hoped to address such challenges through bolstering regional collaboration between Indigenous Peoples.




Hamilton said there have been discussions about holding a Pacific region meeting before future UN events. 




This would help save their communities’ limited resources by working out shared strategies ahead of time — and help ensure that delegates are “not coming here with competing interests, or we’re really clear on what our common interests are.”




“We’ve got to try and balance immediate economic interests with longer-term environmental protections,” she said. 




“I think we’ve got a responsibility to protect our descendants.”







READ MORE:

 

‘Very concerned’: UN Indigenous Peoples forum impacted by ongoing funding crisis







The 

UN Voluntary Fund for Indigenous Peoples

, which helps finance participants’ travels to UN forums, is also experiencing budget shortfalls, inhibiting many delegates’ ability to attend international events.




The fund is seen as an important way to help delegates attend from areas where governments do not recognize the citizens within their borders as Indigenous.




Sheryl Lightfoot, EMRIP’s “North America” region representative, is an Anishinaabe expert in Indigenous rights, global politics, and public policy, and previously served as the Canada Research Chair in Global Indigenous Rights and Politics. 




The University of Toronto political science professor noted that states are not involved in how EMRIP officially recognizes Indigenous Peoples.




“Worldwide, there’s a need … of Indigenous peoples seeking just mere recognition of their existence from their governments,” she said.




“States seem to be more resistant now than they were 10 years ago to recognize that peoples are Indigenous peoples and have those rights attached to them.”




Kenneth Deer argued the reason some states refuse to recognize Indigenous identity within their borders is purely “political.”




“There are peoples who are obviously Indigenous,” he said, “but states do not want to recognize them as Indigenous for their own purposes.




“They don’t want to have the peoples having a right to self-determination — and that seems to be a big problem for some states.”




Sheryl Lightfoot, an Anishinaabe expert on international Indigenous rights, represents ‘North America’ on EMRIP expert panel. 

Photo by Dionne Phillips




From climate to tech, new crises emerge




The destruction of lands — from deforestation in South America, to ice-melt in the Arctic, or the water and energy needed to feed artificial intelligence (AI) data centres — add to the long list of threats to Indigenous communities worldwide.




“Indigenous peoples are usually on the frontlines of those events that are happening so quickly around us,” Lightfoot said.




“And so livelihoods are impacted, economies are impacted, and people’s traditional and spiritual ways are impacted.”




That’s especially the case in the development of AI, Deer warned — which many Indigenous leaders have criticized as a 

new form of extractive industry

.




“We have to learn how to protect ourselves [and] protect our traditional knowledge,” he argued.




“Because AI can take that traditional knowledge and send it anywhere, everywhere, and change it.”







READ MORE:

 

AI data centers are booming. Indigenous People want help protecting their lands and knowledge







For Hamilton, regulating AI shouldn’t only be about protecting traditional knowledge or data sovereignty; EMRIP should also consider the technology’s global environmental harms.




“One thing that was disappointing for me was really that a lot of the discussion in there focused on the positives and data sovereignty and data governance and ethics,” she said, “but very few also incorporated the climate impacts.”




Lightfoot agreed new technologies have wrought massive uncertainty — developments unforeseen when UNDRIP was signed nearly 20 years ago.




“This is something we could have never imagined in 2007,” she said. “That kind of technology didn’t exist yet — or at least we didn’t know that it existed. 




“So these are new questions that keep coming forward.”




The United Nations headquarters in Geneva. 

Photo by Dionne Phillips




From ‘valuable input’ — to expert consensus




Lightfoot emphasized that EMRIP is a space for Indigenous delegates to talk freely and openly on any issues that affect them.




This encourages often-differing perspectives, and therefore offers UN agencies “valuable input” on how to better implement UNDRIP. 




“Our job then is to come away, take a look at all of those inputs, examine the Declaration — not any particular articles necessarily, but as a whole,” she explained. 




“We take a look at the Declaration, and as experts, then we’re supposed to offer some advice on what alignment with the Declaration means for that issue area.”




Lightfoot explained that, after discussions among EMRIP’s seven appointed experts, their challenge then is to reach consensus on what formal recommendations they will issue. 




As extractive industries expand their reach and techniques — and AI continues its rapid evolution — delegates agreed there remains considerable uncertainty on how to make progress towards Indigenous rights in the coming era.







READ MORE:

 

AI is a double-edged sword for Indigenous stewardship, say UN experts







“What we’re seeing in a lot of our countries is regression of human and Indigenous rights,” Hamilton warned. 




As Deer sees it, he’s witnessed many caucuses of Indigenous delegates at the UN doing important collaborations. 




But he wishes they could have a higher profile — and find ways to participate in international decision-making, bringing their voice to the tables of power where it is needed.




“Indigenous peoples want to have a voice,” he said. “They want to be heard.”




Having diverse voices at the UN’s highest levels, he believes, would in fact improve the overall UN processes and system — to the benefit of all countries.




“What we need is the states, now, to agree to a process that was run by Indigenous people,” he said.




For Hamilton, hearing other Indigenous people from around the globe speak about how they’ve persevered through hardships has helped inspire and restore her hope, despite all the crises and challenges.




“I feel like there’s a real sense of … urgency and concern,” she said. 




“We don’t want our grandchildren’s grandchildren to have to keep coming here and doing this stuff.”

content:
Mar 4, 2026 | Documenter l'extrême-droite

L’ex-olympien Giulio Zardo, de Montréal, a été identifié comme un membre sympathisant et facilitateur du groupuscule néonazi Frontenac Active Club.

Le 3 mars, The Tyee, un média indépendant basé en Colombie-Britannique, publiait un article de la journaliste Rachel Gilmore démontrant que les activistes du Frontenac Active Club (FAC) se sont régulièrement entraînés dans un gym de Saint-Léonard, Alpha Athletika, à l’invitation d’un ex-olympien, Giulio Zardo, qui y était employé comme coach.

Pour lire l’article (en anglais) –> How a White Nationalist Club Thought It Found Safe Haven in a Montreal Gym

Nous nous réjouissons de la parution de cet article et remercions Rachel pour son travail, en espérant que d’autres journalistes prennent enfin ces sujets au sérieux.

Les administrateurs du gym ont assuré Rachel Gilmore qu’ils n’étaient pas du tout au courant de cette situation, que les séances d’entraînement du FAC (documentés sur la chaîne Telegram du groupuscule) se sont déroulées en dehors des heures régulières d’ouverture, et qu’ils ont congédié Giulio Zardo sur-le-champ lorsqu’ils en ont été informés. Nous n’avons aucune raison de douter de leur bonne foi.

L’article démontre de manière convaincante que Zardo lui-même a participé à ces entraînements et posé pour les photos de propagande du groupe suprémaciste blanc. Nous avions déjà mentionné Giulio Zardo dans un article de 2021 sur les révélations que nous avait faites un sketchbag de l’entourage d’Atalante Québec, mais n’avions jamais trouvé de preuves concluantes de sa participation active au milieu néofasciste québécois. C’est maintenant chose faite.

Giulio Zardo s’entraîne au Alpha Athletika de Saint-Léonard, où il était embauché comme coach jusqu’au 3 mars 2026. Dans la photo de droite, on aperçoit Shawn Beauvais MacDonald, le leader de facto du Frontenac Active Club. Photo tirée de l’article du Tyee.

Rachel Gilmore et Elizabeth Simons (Canadian Anti-Hate Network) ont identifié Giulio Zardo sur les photos de propagande publiées sur la chaîne Telegram du Frontenac Active Club. Photo tirée de l’article du Tyee.
